newsitem.title: USA: AT&T's Walter resigns; had been heir-apparent.
newsitem.headline: AT&T's Walter resigns; had been heir-apparent.

text.p: John Walter, tapped nine months ago to become chairman of AT&T Corp., abruptly resigned Wednesday after the board of directors declined to give him the promised promotion, the company said.

The nation's largest long-distance phone company said its board voted not to promote Walter to chief executive officer, succeeding Robert Allen. At the time of his appointment last October, some industry officials wondered whether Walter, former chairman of printer R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co., would be able to lead AT&T effectively in the highly competitive telecommunications market.

Walter, 50, appointed in October, joined AT&T last November and was expected to succeed Allen as CEO in January 1998. The resignation came after the board decided it was not ready to name him CEO on the schedule originally discussed, the company said.
In a conference call with reporters, AT&T director Walter Elisha said the decision came after months of consideration.

"It may well have been that we erred in bringing him in the first place," Elisha said in response to a reporter's question about the decision to hire Walter as Allen's heir apparent last year. Elisha is chairman of textile maker Springs Industries Inc. and a spokesman for AT&T's eight independent directors.

The resignation followed months of speculation that Walter might be passed over as Allen's successor if AT&T's reported merger talks with SBC Communications Inc. led to a merger. SBC Chairman Ed Whiteacre was said to be in line to replace Allen as head of the combined company. But the talks have lost momentum, industry sources said.
The AT&T board also said a special committee would conduct a search for a CEO and recommend a successor. Allen has agreed to remain as chairman and CEO while the search is conducted, Elisha said.

It also named John Zeglis, 50, only recently named vice chairman, to head AT&T operations, making him one of the likely candidates for the CEO position. Zeglis had been AT&T's chief corporate counsel and head of government affairs.
Investors greeted the news with enthusiasm, and AT&T stock jumped $1.31 to $36.31 on the New York Stock Exchange.
In AT&T's statement, Walter said his plans were uncertain. "I believe I am perfectly qualified to be CEO of AT&T right now," he said. "I have worked tirelessly on behalf of the shareholders of AT&T."

Under his contract with AT&T, Walter, who also resigned as a director of the company, will receive about $3.8 million in severance pay, in addition to the $22 million compensation package AT&T provided when he left Donnelley.

Elisha said the board's action came after discussions among the eight independent directors at meetings Tuesday night and Wednesday morning. The eight directors voted unamiously not to elect Walter according to the original schedule, and Walter resigned at a meeting Wednesday morning.

Robert Allen took part in the initial part of the Tuesday meeting but was not present during the discussions leading to the vote, Elisha said. Allen had recommended to the board that they not elect Walter to become chief executive in January.
The board member said Allen had expressed reservations at monthly meetings with board members since April.
